items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like Benny Goodman, Chu Berry, Dizzy Gillespie. They all had a sound that they could be recognized.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. Regardless what he played when he was there, you miss © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

seeing him. He had an aura about him that everybody loved. Everybody loved Count Basie. Everybody loved Duke Ellington. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So, there were so many playing their style, so you’d get confused. Tonight you would hear Lester, the next night you would hear Chu Berry...

ctx.x: Sinatra record, it could be on a sound track, it could be on a jazz recording and you know immediately it’s you.

I’ve tried to be original and as I said before, everybody in my era, they were identifiable. Nobody sounds like Benny Carter, he’s got a sound of his own. Nobody sounded like Chu Berry, nobody sounded like Art Tatum. Nobody sounded alike in that era, period. You can’t name anybody that sounded alike in that era that I was coming up. So, I was just following a trend, I was just trying to be original myself, trying to play the only way I knew how and that was, like Basie used to say, “If you don’t know the chords…
Could you say that Basie’s piano actually had some effect on your developing this trumpet style.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: He respected Chu Berry, he respected Joe Thomas.

ctx.x: Oh, Lester. He didn't like nobody's playing but his. He loved his playing. He respected Coleman
Hawkins, give him all the respect in the world. He respected Chu Berry, he respected Joe Thomas. But he liked his playing. He liked his playing.
And everything he did was a classic. Like he had names for different people. He nicknamed Basie, "Holy," the Holy Man, because he was the leader.
